title: Laughing at yourself
hook: Nasruddin searches under the lamp; Montaigne sides with laughing Democritus over weeping Heraclitus
tomorrow: who was told "touch me not" on a morning of pure joy?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: feast. A holy man called a glutton, because his table was the welcome. Today, what happens when the feast goes wrong.

Everybody has a moment they'd rather nobody had seen. A story told about Mulla Nasruddin, the wise fool of the folk tales: a neighbor finds him on his knees under a streetlamp. What did you lose? My key. They both search. Nothing. Where exactly did you drop it? In my house. Then why look out here? Because, says Nasruddin, there's more light here.
screen: `THE MOMENT NOBODY SHOULD SEE.` → `NASRUDDIN UNDER THE LAMP.` → `THERE'S MORE LIGHT HERE.`

segments.voice: The joke is on Nasruddin, and then it's on us: we search where it's comfortable, not where we lost it. That's how these teaching tales work: you laugh at the fool, then recognize yourself. That's one side of today's debate: laughing at yourself is wisdom. Montaigne, the French essayist, took that side. In his essay on Democritus and Heraclitus, he sets two old philosophers side by side. Democritus laughed at human life; Heraclitus wept over it. Montaigne prefers the laugher: we are, he says, less unhappy than vain, more foolish than wicked, and laughing at that takes us less seriously than weeping does. Now the other side, at its best. Heraclitus's tears aren't silly. Some mistakes hurt people, and a laugh can be a way of dodging the repair. Tears take the damage seriously. The weeper's best case: don't make a joke of what needs fixing. The laughers can answer: laughing at yourself isn't laughing off what you did to someone else. It's refusing to make your own dignity the center of the universe. And one more look at the joke: Nasruddin never stops searching. He just admits where he's looking.
screen: `MORE LIGHT OUT HERE.` · `DEMOCRITUS LAUGHS, HERACLITUS WEEPS.` · `MONTAIGNE TAKES THE LAUGHER.` · `THE WEEPER'S BEST CASE.` · then, large: `LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Recall one recent moment you got wrong in a harmless, human way: a dropped plate, a wrong name, a door you pushed that said pull. Tell it to yourself like a Nasruddin story, out loud if you can, and let a smile come if it wants to.
Laughing at yourself: seeing your own fumbles with a smile, the Nasruddin and Montaigne way, without laughing off harm.
Your line: laugh. The fool under the streetlamp is all of us, now and then. Back tomorrow.
